title: Object survives, relation disappears: asymmetrical survival in microscope-slide archives
research_problem: Survival is usually treated as a binary property of the object. The source survey shows that physical slides, instruments, labels, indexes, transaction records, working papers, publication crosswalks and original collection order survive independently. A slide may survive while the relation that once made it intelligible does not, and the reverse is also possible.
working_claim: The historical recoverability of a microscope preparation depends on at least three independent survivals: the object, the documentary apparatus, and the crosswalk connecting them. Collection history is therefore partly a history of relation survival, not simply object preservation.

survival_pattern.physical_slides: strong for at least one near-complete private set; institutional examples unresolved
survival_pattern.original_publication_crosswalk: recoverable from numbering and contemporary descriptions but vulnerable after cabinet/library separation

cases.lesson: The book can survive perfectly while the glass component becomes bibliographically invisible. Object and print survival do not guarantee survival of the relation that made them one publication.
Later cataloguing can preserve obsolete addresses rather than overwrite them. This is a positive-control case for relation survival.
Instrument survival can coexist with loss of the maker's operational paper trail. Downstream archives can document later use without restoring the missing maker-level chain.
All major components can survive while the original working collection ceases to exist as a retrievable whole. Preservation by specialization can produce relational loss.

survival_pattern.labels: rich experimental/publication/remounting information survives on object

cases.lesson: The object label can carry enough documentary information to bridge institutional separation after a scientist's papers and preparations diverge.
A maintained crosswalk allows a collection to change storage, institution and database without severing the series from its documentary apparatus.
Material residues can preserve cabinet ecology even when provenance is weak. Broken slides and loose papers should be treated as evidence of maintenance and use rather than discarded as noise.

survival_types.research_strategy: extract material traces, labels, repairs and later-use records; make the documentary gap explicit
reconstruct historical system from records while refusing to claim surviving object continuity without a physical match
model identifier transitions and relation preservation at item level
reconstruct the former relational system across present repositories

method_consequences: Do not use 'survives' as a single field. Record what survives and at what relational level.
A later catalogue that preserves old numbers is historical evidence of deliberate relation maintenance.
A missing crosswalk is not merely a data deficiency; it may be the result of institutional reclassification, transfer, binding, reboxing or disciplinary division.
A destroyed archive should not be backfilled from later secondary reconstructions without marking the inferential distance.
Broken slides, remounting notes, replacement objects and empty cabinet slots can be evidence of use and maintenance.
Digital cataloguing is a new survival event: it can recombine formerly separated identifiers, but may also flatten historical namespaces if poorly designed.
